query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A functionally graded high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating that integrates a hard, wear‐resistant top layer with an oxidation- and corrosion‐protective sub-layer will exhibit superior tribo‐corrosion degradation resistance at elevated temperatures compared to conventional uniform HEA coatings or standard structural alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A standard structural substrate (e.g., 42-CrMo steel) with no prior surface treatment or coating.
generation.intervention: Apply a multilayer HEA coating via surface engineering techniques (such as laser cladding) where the top layer is formulated for high hardness and low friction (e.g., a W-based HEA with controlled Cr content) and the underlying sub-layer is engineered for enhanced oxidation and corrosion resistance.
generation.conditions: Exposure to elevated temperatures (approximately 450–650°C) in a corrosive environment (e.g., NaCl-containing medium) under dynamic mechanical sliding conditions that induce tribo‐corrosion.
generation.structural_mediator: The graded multilayer structure, with a refined grain size and controlled interdiffusion at the interface, which promotes the generation of a stable, protective oxide layer enriched in oxidation‐resistant elements in the sub-layer while maintaining a wear‐resistant top surface.
generation.mechanism: The wear-resistant top layer minimizes mechanical damage during sliding, reducing friction and dislocation-induced degradation, while the sub-layer forms and maintains a protective oxide scale at high temperature, mitigating corrosion. The functionally graded interface ensures good adhesion and minimizes spallation, thereby synergistically combating tribo‐corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The multilayer HEA coating is expected to exhibit reduced wear rates, lower friction coefficients, and decreased corrosion (oxidation) rates, leading to an overall significant extension in component lifespan under harsh tribo‐corrosive conditions compared to conventional coatings.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics from conventional uniform HEA coatings (e.g., a uniform W-based HEA with constant Cr content) or standard structural alloys such as duplex stainless steels tested under similar conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement may be limited if the designed layer thicknesses or interdiffusion barriers are not optimized, especially when exposed to temperatures or mechanical stresses that exceed the engineered limits (e.g., above 650°C or with extreme friction forces), potentially leading to coating delamination.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal compositions, layer thicknesses, and the quantitative extent of performance enhancement remain uncertain and require systematic experimental tuning. The precise interplay between friction-induced temperature rise and oxide layer stability during dynamic sliding conditions also needs further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens on 42-CrMo steel substrates: one set with the proposed functionally graded multilayer HEA coating and a control set with a conventional single-layer HEA coating. Subject both sets to cyclic tribo‐corrosion testing in a high-temperature (450–650°C) chamber with a 3.5 wt% NaCl atmosphere under controlled sliding wear conditions.
measurements: Quantitative wear rate (mass loss per area and friction coefficient over time)
Corrosion/oxidation rate (measure weight gain and oxide scale formation)
Microstructural integrity of the coating layers (using SEM and XRD pre- and post-test)
Adhesion and delamination check between layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the functionally graded multilayer coating does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than approximately 15% lower wear and corrosion rates) relative to the conventional single-layer coating, or if the coating shows premature delamination/failure under the test conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. decision.trend: Early work on refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) has emphasized improving high-temperature mechanical strength and oxidation/corrosion resistance (PMC7513042), for example by incorporating hard ceramic particles (TiC, Al2O3) into NbMoCrTiAl-based alloys. More recent efforts leverage tungsten-based HEA coatings with controlled Cr additions to enhance oxidation and corrosion behavior (PMC10142552). Despite these advances, specific studies targeting tribological performance in corrosive, high-temperature conditions remain limited.
decision.unsolved: Although mechanical properties and corrosion resistance have separately advanced, the combined challenge of wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures—tribo-corrosion—remains underexplored. Integrating both wear and corrosion resistance in a robust alloy system or surface treatment is still an open issue, especially under extreme service conditions.
decision.lever: Adopt a multilayer or functionally graded high-entropy alloy coating strategy that integrates a hard, wear-resistant top layer with an oxidation- and corrosion-protective sub-layer. Control factors include layer thickness, interdiffusion barriers, and stable oxide-forming elements for sustained tribo-corrosion protection.
decision.why: Building on prior successes in improving high-temperature strength, oxidation, and corrosion resistance, the next logical step is to address tribo-corrosion via targeted surface engineering. A carefully designed graded or layered HEA coating can modulate friction and wear in corrosive media at elevated temperatures, thereby tackling the untreated challenge of concurrent mechanical and chemical degradation.
